## Where We're Headed

*From what an AI assistant actually is, to the four ways people build one.*

1. **What is conversational AI?** — the building blocks: intent, entity, dialogue, and orchestration
2. **The conversational AI ecosystem** — rule-based, retrieval-based, generative, and task-oriented systems
3. **Building your first assistant** — a worked example: Fictitious Inc.'s customer service skill
4. **Confidence & control** — how an assistant knows when it doesn't know

## What Is Conversational AI? {background-color="#BA0C2F"}

::: {.kicker}
PART ONE
:::

*Before the ecosystem, the fundamentals: what these systems are built from.*

## Three Types of AI Assistants

*Alan Freed's Conversational AI (Manning) distinguishes assistants by what they're built to do.*

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.tag-cardinal}
**Conversational AI**

Answers questions and holds back-and-forth exchanges, from a simple fact lookup to a multi-turn diagnostic conversation.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
**Command Interpreter**

Executes a specific action the user requests, gathering only the parameters needed to complete it.
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
**Event Classifier**

Categorizes an incoming message so it can be routed or acted on, without necessarily replying conversationally.
:::
:::

*Freed, A. (2021). Conversational AI. Manning Publications, Ch. 1.*

## The Baseline Interaction: Simple Q&A

*A question is asked, an answer is given, and the request is complete.*

::: {.callout}
**"What is the coronavirus?"** — In Freed's CDC assistant example, this gets a static, descriptive answer. No API call is needed, so the interface, NLU, and dialogue engine handle it entirely on their own.
:::

**Not every simple answer is static:** "How many COVID cases are there?" also gets a one-line answer — but the number changes daily. An orchestrator queries a live case-count API each time, even though the response format stays simple.

## When a Simple Answer Isn't Enough {background-color="#BA0C2F"}

*"Do I have the coronavirus?" can't be answered in one line — it needs a process.*

::: {.callout}
A static result here would run pages long and put all the interpretive work on the user. Instead, the assistant asks follow-up questions — about fever, then breathing difficulty — and only delivers a recommendation once it has enough information.
:::

1. **Greeting**
2. **Recognize the question, start a process flow**
3. **Ask follow-up questions one at a time**
4. **Give a final, informed recommendation**

## Command Interpreters: A Different Kind of Assistant

*Not every AI assistant holds a conversation — some just execute a command.*

::: {.callout}
"Set an alarm for 9 p.m." is a command, not a question — there's no back-and-forth needed once the system has everything it needs to act.
:::

- **Commands are intents; parameters are entities** — the terminology shifts slightly, but the underlying structure is the same
- **Missing a parameter triggers a follow-up** — "Set an alarm" recognizes the command but asks for the missing time
- **All parameters at once ends the exchange** — supplying time and label together executes immediately

## The Architecture Behind the Conversation {background-color="#003B5C"}

*Four components recur across nearly every conversational AI platform.*

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="25%"}
::: {.tag-cardinal}
**Interface**

What the user types or speaks into.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="25%"}
::: {.tag-cardinal}
**NLU**

Turns text into a recognized intent and entities.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="25%"}
::: {.tag-cardinal}
**Dialogue Engine**

Decides how to respond based on state.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="25%"}
::: {.tag-cardinal}
**Orchestrator**

Calls external APIs for live data.
:::
:::
:::

*Freed, A. (2021). Conversational AI. Manning Publications, Ch. 1–2.*

## Walking Through One Turn: Setting an Alarm

*An original diagram tracing Freed's alarm example through all four architecture components.*

```{mermaid}
%%{init: {'theme':'base', 'themeVariables': {'primaryColor':'#BA0C2F','primaryTextColor':'#fff','primaryBorderColor':'#7A0A22','lineColor':'#C0AC7E'}}}%%
flowchart LR
    I["Interface"] --> N["NLU"]
    N --> D["Dialogue Engine"]
    D --> O["Orchestrator"]
    style I fill:#003B5C,color:#fff
    style N fill:#BA0C2F,color:#fff
    style D fill:#7A0A22,color:#fff
    style O fill:#8A2A0E,color:#fff
```

| Step | What happens |
|---|---|
| **1. User speaks** | "Set an alarm for 9 p.m." |
| **2. Interface → NLU** | Passes the raw utterance along for understanding |
| **3. NLU responds** | Intent: set_alarm · Entity: 9 p.m. |
| **4. Dialogue engine decides** | Looks up the response for set_alarm + a time |
| **5. Orchestrator acts** | Calls the alarm API to actually set 9 p.m. |
| **6. Assistant replies** | "I've set an alarm for 9 p.m." |

## The Conversational AI Ecosystem {background-color="#003B5C"}

::: {.kicker}
PART TWO
:::

*Four fundamentally different approaches to building a system that talks back.*

## Four Approaches to Building a Conversational System

*Two well-established surveys of the field converge on this same basic map.*

| | |
|---|---|
| **Rule-Based** | Hand-written patterns and scripted responses |
| **Retrieval-Based** | Selects the best-fitting response from a fixed pool |
| **Generative** | Composes a novel response, word by word |
| **Task-Oriented** | Optimized to complete a specific goal, not just chat |

::: {.callout}
**Two axes, not one list:** Chen et al. (2017) and Gao et al. (2019) both frame this as two separate questions: what is the system trying to do, and how does it generate what it says.
:::

## Rule-Based Systems: Where It All Began

*1966 · The first chatbot ran on nothing but pattern matching.*

::: {.callout}
Joseph Weizenbaum's ELIZA, built at MIT, simulated a Rogerian psychotherapist using hand-crafted scripts. It searched the user's last message for keywords and reflected them back as a question, following rules a person had written in advance.
:::

**A lineage still visible today:** every rule-based system since ELIZA shares its core idea. The command interpreter from Part 1 is a modern, structured descendant of the same basic approach.

*Weizenbaum, J. (1966). ELIZA. Communications of the ACM, 9(1), 36–45.*

## Rule-Based Systems, Formalized {background-color="#003B5C"}

*1995 · AIML turns ELIZA's ad hoc scripts into a reusable markup language.*

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.tag-cardinal}
**ALICE and AIML**

Richard Wallace's A.L.I.C.E. chatbot used a new XML-based language, AIML, to define patterns and templates. ALICE's knowledge base grew to roughly 41,000 categories, versus ELIZA's roughly 200, and won the Loebner Prize three times.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Strengths and limits**

- **Predictable and controllable** — every response is human-written
- **Brittle outside its scripts** — anything unanticipated isn't handled well
- **Labor-intensive to scale** — more topics means more hand-written rules
:::
:::

## Retrieval-Based Chatbots: Selecting, Not Creating

*Instead of writing rules by hand, retrieve the best existing response.*

::: {.callout}
A retrieval-based system is given a large corpus of candidate responses and selects the one that best fits the current context. Chen et al. (2017) note this tends to produce fluent, natural-sounding replies, because every response was, at some point, actually said by a person.
:::

**The trade-off:** a retrieval-based system can only ever say something already in its response pool — it cannot compose a genuinely new sentence.

## How Retrieval Systems Work {background-color="#7A0A22"}

*Three steps, whether the matching is simple keyword overlap or a modern neural encoder.*

1. **Encode the context** — represent the current conversation in a comparable form
2. **Score every candidate** — compare the context to each response in the pool
3. **Return the best match** — select and return the highest-scoring candidate, unmodified

## Generative Models & LLMs: Composing Novel Responses

*No fixed pool of answers — the response is built one word at a time.*

::: {.callout}
A generative model produces new text token by token, conditioned on the conversation so far. Chen et al. describe the appeal directly: generative models can produce responses that could never have appeared anywhere in a training corpus.
:::

**The trade-off:** because nothing constrains the output to a pre-approved set, generative systems can also produce something inconsistent, off-topic, or wrong.

## From Seq2Seq to ChatGPT {background-color="#003B5C"}

*The generative lineage, in three jumps.*

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.tag-cardinal}
**2014–2017**

Neural sequence models learned to generate responses directly from data.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.tag-cardinal}
**2017**

The Transformer became the foundation for every major LLM since.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.tag-cardinal}
**2022**

ChatGPT brought generative chat to a mass audience.
:::
:::
:::

## Retrieval vs. Generative, Side by Side {.smaller}

*The same underlying trade-off Chen et al. (2017) identify, made concrete.*

| | Retrieval-Based | Generative |
|---|---|---|
| **Response source** | An existing pool of real, human-written text | Composed fresh, token by token |
| **Fluency** | Reliably fluent | Usually fluent, but can drift |
| **Novelty** | Never says anything outside its pool | Can respond to unseen situations |
| **Main risk** | No good match for unusual input | Can generate incorrect content |
| **Typical use** | Customer service, known topics | Open-ended chat, drafting |

## Task-Oriented Dialogue Systems {background-color="#BA0C2F"}

*A different question entirely: not how to generate text, but what the conversation is for.*

::: {.callout}
Chen et al. (2017) split dialogue systems along a second axis: task-oriented systems help a user accomplish something concrete, versus non-task-oriented systems built for open-ended chat. A task-oriented system can be built with rule-based, retrieval-based, or generative techniques underneath.
:::

**Success looks different, too:** a task-oriented system is judged on whether the task got done — not conversational charm.

## The Task-Oriented Pipeline

*Mapping Freed's architecture from Part 1 onto the standard task-oriented pipeline.*

| Stage | Freed's Term | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| **NLU** | Interface + NLU | Recognize the intent and entities |
| **Dialogue State** | Dialogue Engine | Track what's been established so far |
| **Policy** | Dialogue Engine + Orchestrator | Decide the next action |
| **Response** | Interface | Generate or select the reply |

::: {.callout}
Modern systems increasingly blend these approaches: a task-oriented assistant might use an LLM to generate phrasing, while still following rule-based logic to decide when a task is complete.
:::

## Building Your First Conversational AI {background-color="#BA0C2F"}

::: {.kicker}
PART THREE
:::

*Freed's worked example: a fictitious company builds a customer-service skill from scratch.*

## Meet Fictitious Inc.

*A concrete, worked example — building a store-hours-and-locations assistant.*

::: {.callout}
Freed's textbook walks through building a customer-service assistant for a fictional retail company. The goal is small and concrete: answer questions about store hours and locations.
:::

**Why start this small:** a narrow, well-defined scope lets you see the entire pipeline — intent recognition, entity extraction, dialogue response — working end to end, before adding slots, multi-turn flows, or live API calls.

*Freed, A. (2021). Conversational AI. Manning Publications, Ch. 2.*

## Two Building Blocks: Assistant and Skill {background-color="#003B5C"}

*Watson Assistant's terms for the interface layer and the dialogue engine, made concrete.*

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.tag-cardinal}
**Assistant**

The interface layer — what the end user actually talks to, and where the finished experience is deployed.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.tag-cardinal}
**Skill**

The dialogue engine underneath — the collection of intents, entities, and dialogue nodes.
:::
:::
:::

## Training Intents

*An intent is trained by example, not by writing exhaustive rules.*

::: {.callout}
An intent like #store_hours is trained with a handful of example phrases — "What time do you open?", "When are you open today?" — not an exhaustive list of every possible phrasing.
:::

**The testing interface:** Freed's walkthrough uses Watson Assistant's built-in tester to try new phrasings and see which intent is recognized, and how confident the system is.

**Confidence is a probability, not a guarantee:** every recognized intent comes with a confidence value between 0 and 1.

## Responding with Dialogue Nodes {background-color="#BA0C2F"}

*The dialogue engine matches a recognized intent to a node that defines what to say back.*

- **Welcome** — fires automatically at the start of a new conversation
- **#store_hours** — fires whenever that intent is recognized, returning the appropriate response
- **Anything Else** — a fallback that catches input matching no intent with sufficient confidence

## Anatomy of a Dialogue Node Tree

*An original diagram of how one recognized intent branches into store-specific replies.*

```{mermaid}
%%{init: {'theme':'base', 'themeVariables': {'primaryColor':'#BA0C2F','primaryTextColor':'#fff','primaryBorderColor':'#7A0A22','lineColor':'#C0AC7E'}}}%%
flowchart TD
    R["#store_location
    intent recognized"] --> E["@store_location: Elm
    'The Elm store is at
    456 Elm Drive.'"]
    R --> M["@store_location: Maple
    'The Maple store is at
    123 Maple Street.'"]
    R --> A["Anything Else (no entity)
    'We have two locations —
    Elm and Maple.'"]
    style R fill:#BA0C2F,color:#fff
    style E fill:#003B5C,color:#fff
    style M fill:#7A0A22,color:#fff
    style A fill:#8A2A0E,color:#fff
```

::: {.callout}
This is the *n + 2* pattern Freed describes: one child node per unique entity value, plus one fallback for when the intent is recognized but no entity is present.
:::

## Adding Entities for Context

*An intent tells you what the user wants; an entity tells you the specifics.*

::: {.callout}
"What time does the Boston store open?" recognizes the #store_hours intent, plus a @store_location entity valued "Boston." The dialogue node can now respond with hours for that specific location.
:::

**Fuzzy matching handles the real world:** entities configured with fuzzy matching let "Bosten" or "boston, ma" still resolve to the same value — without a hand-written rule for every misspelling.

## Slots for Multi-Parameter Requests {background-color="#003B5C"}

*An original flowchart of the slot-filling loop — ask, check, repeat until done.*

::: {.callout}
"I'd like to book an appointment" supplies an intent but no details. Freed's example uses slots to define every entity needed — date, time, service type — and asks a targeted follow-up for each one still missing.
:::

```{mermaid}
%%{init: {'theme':'base', 'themeVariables': {'primaryColor':'#BA0C2F','primaryTextColor':'#fff','primaryBorderColor':'#7A0A22','lineColor':'#C0AC7E'}}}%%
flowchart TD
    S["'Book an appointment'"] --> Q{"All slots
    filled?"}
    Q -->|No| F["Ask for the missing slot
    'What day would you
    like to come in?'"]
    F --> Q
    Q -->|Yes| C["Confirm the appointment
    'Set for Maple,
    9:15 AM, Friday.'"]
    style S fill:#BA0C2F,color:#fff
    style Q fill:#FAF8F5,color:#333
    style F fill:#BA0C2F,color:#fff
    style C fill:#8A2A0E,color:#fff
```

## Confidence Thresholds & the Two-Strikes Rule

*How an assistant knows when it doesn't know — and what it does about it.*

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.tag-cardinal}
**A confidence threshold**

Freed's walkthrough sets a minimum confidence value — below it, the system treats the intent as unrecognized, even if it was the highest-scoring guess.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**The two-strikes rule**

The first low-confidence input gets a clarifying response. A second consecutive low-confidence input escalates further — for example, to a human agent.
:::
:::

## The Two-Strikes Rule, as a Flowchart {background-color="#7A0A22"}

*An original flowchart of Freed's escalation logic — low-confidence guesses accumulate toward a handoff.*

```{mermaid}
%%{init: {'theme':'base', 'themeVariables': {'primaryColor':'#BA0C2F','primaryTextColor':'#fff','primaryBorderColor':'#7A0A22','lineColor':'#C0AC7E'}}}%%
flowchart TD
    U["User utterance received"] --> D1{"Confidence ≥
    threshold?"}
    D1 -->|Yes| R["Respond normally;
    reset strike count to 0"]
    D1 -->|No| INC["Increment
    misunderstood_count"]
    INC --> D2{"Count ≥ 2
    (two strikes)?"}
    D2 -->|No| ASK["'I didn't understand.
    Can you try rephrasing?'"]
    D2 -->|Yes| ESC["Escalate: offer a human
    agent or another channel"]
    style U fill:#BA0C2F,color:#fff
    style D1 fill:#FAF8F5,color:#333
    style D2 fill:#FAF8F5,color:#333
    style R fill:#8A2A0E,color:#fff
    style INC fill:#003B5C,color:#fff
    style ASK fill:#BA0C2F,color:#fff
    style ESC fill:#7A0A22,color:#fff
```

## Discussion Questions {background-color="#003B5C" .smaller}

*Bring your answers to at least one of these to class.*

1. Pick an AI assistant you use regularly. Which of the four approaches best describes how it likely works, and why?
2. Chen et al. argue retrieval-based systems are more fluent but less flexible than generative ones. Can you think of a task where that trade-off would matter enormously?
3. Freed's two-strikes rule escalates to a human after two low-confidence guesses. What would the right threshold be for your own course project's assistant?
4. Modern LLM-based assistants blend rule-based logic, retrieval (e.g., RAG), and generation together. Pick a real product and try to identify all three pieces in it.

## Key Takeaways

*The vocabulary and the map you'll need before Part 2 goes deeper.*

- A conversational AI system is built from the same recurring parts — interface, NLU, dialogue engine, orchestrator — whether answering questions, interpreting commands, or classifying events.
- The conversational AI ecosystem splits along two independent axes: how a response is produced, and what the conversation is for.
- Rule-based systems trace back to ELIZA (1966) and were formalized by AIML (1995); retrieval and generative approaches emerged later, each with real trade-offs, not a strict hierarchy of "better."
- Building even a simple assistant means defining intents, entities, dialogue nodes, and a confidence threshold — vocabulary that scales up to far more sophisticated systems.
